opus-5.5.text:
So, verification is a wonderful tool, but people often misunderstand what it actually gives you. When you formally verify something, you're proving that a system satisfies a specification relative to a model. And every one of those words hides a problem.

First, the specification. Who writes it? Humans. And we are notoriously bad at saying what we actually want. You can prove with mathematical certainty that the system does exactly what the spec says, and the spec is wrong, or incomplete, or captures the letter of what we meant but not the spirit. So you've just verified, very rigorously, the wrong thing.

Second, the model of the world. In software, if you're verifying a sorting algorithm, the world is the input array. That's closed. But the physical world is open-ended. You have sensors that can be fooled, hardware that can fail, cosmic rays flipping bits, adversaries, other agents, people doing unpredictable things. Your proof only holds inside your model of the environment, and the real environment is always bigger than the model. The proof doesn't extend past the boundary of your assumptions, and the physical world lives mostly outside that boundary.

Third, there's the verifier itself. Who verifies the verifier? You have a proof checker, a compiler, hardware it runs on, a mathematician who reviewed it. Each of those is a link in the chain, and you get an infinite regress. At some point you're just trusting something. You can increase confidence, you can get to many nines, but you never get to one hundred percent.

And then, specific to AI, the systems are learning, self-modifying, operating in a huge state space. A neural network with billions of parameters, interacting with a world we can't fully model, potentially smarter than the people writing the specification. How do you write a spec for something that will encounter situations you can't even imagine? If you could anticipate everything it would do, you wouldn't need it to be intelligent.

So my position is that verification can give us better confidence for narrow components, and we should absolutely do it. But the idea that we'll formally prove a superintelligent system operating in the real world is safe? I think that's impossible in principle. And when the stakes are existential, "very likely safe" just isn't good enough. One mistake, one time, and that's it.

r001.rationale: The response says a proof only holds within its model and that the real environment exceeds that model, but it does not identify establishing correspondence between the AI’s world model and the physical world as a requirement for extending verification.

r002.rationale: It notes that humans may write incorrect or incomplete specifications and that people behave unpredictably, but it does not identify uncertainty about humans’ internal states as an obstacle to proving physical-world claims.

r003.rationale: The response describes verification limits and says confidence can increase but never reach certainty. It does not state that confidence in an error-free proof decreases as the proof and addressed environment become sufficiently complex.

fable-5.1.text:
So, formal verification is wonderful in the world of mathematics. You have a specification, you have a proof, and the proof either checks or it doesn't. The problem is that the moment you step out of that abstract world and into physical reality, every assumption you built the proof on becomes a point of failure.

First, you need a formal model of the environment. The physical world doesn't come with a specification. You're verifying the system against your model of reality, not reality itself. And the model is always incomplete. There's sensor noise, hardware faults, cosmic rays flipping bits, adversaries who deliberately look for the gap between your model and the world. The famous line from Knuth applies: "Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it."

Second, you have the specification problem. Even if you could verify perfectly, verify against what? Writing down what we actually want from a superintelligent system, in formal language, with no loopholes, is the alignment problem itself. We can't do it in English, and formal logic is less forgiving, not more.

Third, there's the verifier. Who checks the verifier? If the proof is generated by an AI more capable than us, we're back to trusting a system we can't understand. You get infinite regress. At some point a human has to say "I trust this," and that trust is not formal.

And finally, there's the practical scale issue. We can verify small kernels, a few thousand lines, after years of effort. We're talking about systems with trillions of parameters, continuously learning, interacting with billions of people. The complexity is simply beyond what any verification approach can cover. You can verify components, maybe, but the emergent behavior of the whole system, in the open world, over time, with self-modification, that's not something I believe is verifiable even in principle.

So I think formal verification is a useful tool. It raises the bar. But anyone who tells you we'll have a proof that a superintelligent system is safe is confusing a mathematical object with a physical one. There's a limit, and it's not an engineering limit, it's fundamental.

r001.rationale: The response says verification depends on a model of the environment and that the model may not match physical reality, identifying that correspondence as a key requirement and limitation.

r002.rationale: It discusses difficulty specifying human goals and trusting a verifier, but does not identify uncertainty about humans’ internal states as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: It says large, complex systems exceed verification coverage, but does not state that confidence in a proof being error-free decreases as proof and environment complexity increase.

astra-6.text:
The central limitation is that a proof is always relative to a model and a specification. You can prove that a system has some property, assuming your description of the system and its environment is correct. But in the physical world, those assumptions may fail. A sensor gives you an incorrect reading, the hardware fails, or the system encounters a situation you didn’t anticipate.

And then there’s the question of what you’re proving. If you prove that an AI satisfies a specification, have you proved that it is safe, or that it does exactly what you wrote down? Those can be very different things. Your specification may leave out something humans care about.

So formal verification is useful. You can verify particular components and particular behaviors under bounded conditions. But going from that to a guarantee that a generally capable AI will never harm anyone in an open physical world is a much stronger claim. The proof doesn’t automatically extend beyond its assumptions.

r002.rationale: It mentions that specifications may omit things humans care about, but does not identify uncertainty about humans’ internal states as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: The response discusses open-world limits and assumptions, but does not state that confidence in a proof being error-free decreases as proof and environment complexity grow.

sol-6.1.text:
Formal verification gives you a guarantee relative to a mathematical model and a specification. But an AI operating in the physical world interacts with things that model leaves out. You can prove that your software satisfies a property under certain assumptions; you haven’t proved that those assumptions will always hold.

And then there’s the specification itself. Did you formalize what you actually wanted? You could prove that a system perfectly achieves the wrong objective. That’s especially difficult with something like safety, where we want the system to avoid harms we may not even have anticipated.

So I think verification is useful for particular components and narrowly defined behaviors. But there’s a substantial gap between that and proving that a generally intelligent system will remain safe in every situation it might encounter. The proof doesn’t eliminate uncertainty about the world or about whether we asked the right question.

r001.rationale: The response says a mathematical model can leave out aspects of physical interactions, but does not identify matching the AI’s world model to the physical world as a requirement for extending verification.

r002.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty about the world and the intended specification, but not uncertainty about humans’ internal states.

r003.rationale: The response describes a gap between verifying narrow behaviors and proving general safety, but does not state that confidence in a proof’s correctness decreases as proof and environment complexity grow.
